title: Newsom blasts Trump as billions flow out of state on Tax Day: $275 billion to feds from California
text:
11 hours ago As Tax Day arrives, California leaders are underscoring a stark fiscal reality: the state continues to send far more to Washington, D.C. than it gets back. Officials say California remains the nation’s largest donor state, contributing roughly $275 billion more to the federal government than it receives — more than triple the next closest state.
Photo by Alexander Mils on Unsplash In Sacramento, state leaders framed the imbalance as a growing source of frustration for taxpayers. Governor Gavin Newsom said, “Every year when folks sit down to file their federal taxes, there’s a real sense of frustration — and I feel it too — knowing just how much California sends to Washington and how little we get back. California is the largest donor state in the nation, sending hundreds of billions more to the federal government than we receive. Trump’s incompetence is more salt in the wound.”
The statement also criticizes policies under Donald Trump, pointing to rising costs tied to energy, inflation, and tariffs. According to the administration, Americans are paying more across the board — from gasoline to groceries — while small businesses report supply chain disruptions and declining confidence. The state further claims that federal decisions have contributed to higher housing construction costs and increased monthly utility bills nationwide.
Despite those challenges, California officials argue the state’s economy continues to outperform. Since 2019, California’s gross domestic product has grown by more than $1.18 trillion, surpassing $4 trillion total output and accounting for a significant share of U.S. economic activity. The state has also driven a large portion of growth in publicly traded equities and venture capital investment.
State leaders credit long-term economic strategies, including workforce development and infrastructure investment, for sustaining that growth. With more than 600 colleges and universities and dominance in sectors like technology, health care, and clean energy, California officials maintain the state remains a central engine of the national economy — even as billions continue to flow out each year.
